title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 109
paragraphs: When Themistocles perceived that he would not be able to persuade them — or at least the majority — to sail to the Hellespont, he changed tack and turned to the Athenians (for these were the most grieved at the enemy's escape and were eager to sail to the Hellespont even on their own if the others were unwilling). He spoke to them as follows: “I myself have been present on many occasions before now, and have heard of many more, when something of this sort has happened: men forced into great extremity, after being defeated, fought again and made good their earlier disaster. As for us, since we have won from fortune the continued existence of ourselves and of Greece by repelling so great a cloud of men from our land, let us not pursue enemies who are fleeing from us. For it was not we who accomplished these things, but the gods and heroes, who grudged that one man should be king of both Asia and Europe — a man unholy and presumptuous, who made no distinction between things sacred and things profane, burning and casting down the images of the gods, and who even scourged the sea and let fetters down into it. As things stand, it is good that we now remain in Greece and look to ourselves and our households. Let each man repair his house and attend to the sowing of his land, once we have completely driven away the barbarian; and then, at the beginning of spring, let us sail down toward the Hellespont and Ionia.” He spoke thus intending to lay up a store of gratitude with the Persian, so that if he should meet with any evil at the hands of the Athenians he might have a place of refuge. And that is in fact what came to pass.
